question.problem: What is ${\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
question.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={x}^{4},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{n}=\frac{1}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{1}{n})\,\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{i}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(1+\frac{i}{n})}^{4}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$
